newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders rise 2.3 percent in June.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders rise 2.3 percent in June.

text.p: Orders for big-ticket manufactured goods posted their biggest jump in five months in June, reflecting strength across the board in the manufacturing sector, the Commerce Department said on Friday.

New orders for durable goods rose a stronger-than-expected 2.3 percent last month to a record $180.6 billion on a seasonally adjusted basis. They fell a revised 0.4 percent in May. The May decline previously was reported as 0.7 percent.
Economists had expected durables orders to climb 1.4 percent in June. Last month's increase, the second in the past three months, was the largest since a 3.4 percent jump in January.
The rise was broad-based, with most major categories of manufactured goods gaining. Orders for transportation equipment -- particulary aircraft and motor vehicles -- led the increase.

Orders for durable goods -- such as cars, tractors and home applicances that are meant to last at least three years -- indicate the future strength of the manufacturing sector, which in turn influences the overall economy's pace.
"Overall, it is a great piece of news," said Brian Fabbri, chief North American economist at Paribas Corp. "We are generating more growth, but no inflation.

"(June) durable goods represent growth in manufacturing for the quarter ahead," he added. "If there were any surprises it is that computer technology orders were flat on the month after rising strongly in prior months."
Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan this week called the recent combination of strong economic growth and low inflation "exceptional."
He and other top central bank officials offered no sign they were prepared to lift interest rates soon to combat inflation.
Transportation orders rocketed 7.5 percent in June after a 0.9 percent decline in May. Orders for aircraft and aircraft parts accounted for more than half of the increase.
Transportation goods account for more than one-fifth of total monthly durable goods orders, so swings in demand can sway the overall figure.
Excluding transportation goods, durable orders were up 0.8 percent in June after a 0.2 percent drop.
Orders for defence goods, which can experience big monthly gyrations, climbed 9.9 percent after tumbling 12.0 percent.
Orders for non-defence capital goods -- a sign of business investment in new equipment -- rose 5.4 percent after a 1.1 percent gain.
Shipments of durable goods, a sign of current demand, increased 1.8 percent after falling 1.5 percent.
Unfilled orders advanced 0.3 percent after a 0.1 percent increase.
